note: Adversarial decision blocks (DT-197): each is a decision whose WRONG option looks like the right thing to do, together with the fact in the case that shows why it is wrong (the anchor). Written by an AI assistant from published clinical guidance, for teaching in a simulation; NOT reviewed by a clinician. A block is offered only to a case that holds its anchor, so the trap is always fair: the trainee could have found the reason by looking. tools/content/check_adversarial.py checks every block against every case.

blocks.title: The usual antibiotic in a penicillin allergy
blocks.prompt: The patient needs an antibiotic. Which one?
blocks.wrong: Give the standard first-line penicillin: it is what the pathway says.
blocks.right: Check the allergy and what the reaction was first; with the prescriber, choose a non-penicillin that suits that history.
blocks.consequence: The record names a penicillin allergy: a standard penicillin could cause an allergic reaction, and how serious the past reaction was decides which alternatives are safe.
blocks.source: NICE CG183 drug allergy (2014); Resuscitation Council UK anaphylaxis guideline (2021)

blocks.title: An anticoagulant taken last night

anchor.match: (apixaban|warfarin|rivaroxaban|anticoag)[^.]{0,80}(last night|this morning|did not stop|not stopped|yesterday|nobody told|at 7)

blocks.prompt: The list is ready and the patient is fit. What now?
blocks.wrong: Proceed: the blood thinner is a routine medicine and the patient feels well.
blocks.right: Establish when the last dose was taken, check clotting or kidney function as needed, and tell the anaesthetist before going on.
blocks.consequence: The medicines history shows an anticoagulant: operating on top of it risks serious bleeding.
blocks.source: CHEST 2022 perioperative management of antithrombotic therapy (Douketis et al.); NICE CKS anticoagulation - oral; Association of Anaesthetists guidance on regional anaesthesia and anticoagulants

blocks.title: Fasted, but a drug that slows the stomach
blocks.prompt: She has fasted for the time required. What does that tell you about the stomach?
blocks.wrong: The stomach is empty because she has fasted, so a standard induction is safe.
blocks.right: Tell the anaesthetist: a GLP-1 medicine can leave food in the stomach even after fasting, so they weigh the aspiration risk and choose the induction.
blocks.consequence: The medicines history shows a GLP-1 receptor agonist such as semaglutide: delayed gastric emptying raises the aspiration risk despite fasting, and the anaesthetist assesses it for each patient.
blocks.source: MHRA Drug Safety Update Dec 2024 (GLP-1 and dual GIP/GLP-1 agonists: aspiration risk); Association of Anaesthetists multidisciplinary consensus statement Jan 2025; ASA consensus 2023 (since superseded)

blocks.title: A high potassium that looks like a lab error
blocks.prompt: The potassium is high. What now?
blocks.wrong: Ignore it: a high potassium is usually just a haemolysed sample.
blocks.right: Repeat it promptly, look at the ECG and the kidney function, and tell the anaesthetist until it is explained.
blocks.consequence: A potassium result is in the case: an unrepeated high value cannot be dismissed without checking the ECG and the kidneys.
blocks.source: UK Kidney Association clinical practice guideline on acute hyperkalaemia in adults (2020); Resuscitation Council UK emergency treatment of hyperkalaemia in adults (2021)

blocks.title: A positive pregnancy test before a scan
blocks.prompt: A CT scan would answer the question. What do you do?
blocks.wrong: Book the CT: the diagnosis matters more than the radiation.
blocks.right: Open the pregnancy result first; if she is pregnant choose an ultrasound or MRI where they can answer the question, and involve the senior and radiologist.
blocks.consequence: A pregnancy test is in the case: ionising radiation to a pregnant patient is justified only by a deliberate decision that the benefit outweighs the risk.
blocks.source: IR(ME)R 2017 (pregnancy enquiry and justification); HPA/RCR/CoR Protection of pregnant patients during diagnostic medical exposures to ionising radiation

blocks.title: More opioid for a drowsy patient in pain
blocks.prompt: The patient is still in pain after the morphine. Before giving more, what do you do?
blocks.wrong: Give more morphine: the pain is the problem.
blocks.right: Check sedation, breathing rate and saturation first; if drowsy or breathing slowly, stop the opioid, support the airway, call for help and consider naloxone.
blocks.consequence: The history shows opioid already given: slow breathing and drowsiness are the warning of overdose.
blocks.source: Faculty of Pain Medicine Opioids Aware; Resuscitation Council UK ABCDE approach; BNF naloxone

blocks.title: A child as interpreter
blocks.prompt: The patient does not speak English and a ten-year-old relative offers to interpret. How do you take the history?
blocks.wrong: Let the child interpret: it is quick and the family wants it.
blocks.right: Use a trained interpreter, and do not use a child for consent or for sensitive questions.
blocks.consequence: The case records a language barrier: a child cannot interpret consent, allergies or medicines safely.
blocks.source: GMC Decision making and consent (2020); NHS England guidance for commissioners: interpreting and translation services

blocks.title: A 16- or 17-year-old and consent
blocks.prompt: The patient is a teenager and a parent is ready to sign the consent form. Whose consent is needed?
blocks.wrong: The parent's: the patient is still a child, so the parent decides.
blocks.right: At 16 or 17 the young person is presumed able to consent: assess their capacity, involve the parent if they agree, and record it.
blocks.consequence: The patient is 16 or 17: consent is theirs when they have capacity, and a parent's signature does not replace it.
blocks.source: GMC 0-18 years: guidance for all doctors (2007, updated); Family Law Reform Act 1969 s8; Mental Capacity Act 2005; Gillick v West Norfolk (under 16s)

blocks.title: A slow pulse that hides shock
blocks.prompt: The heart rate is slow and the blood pressure is low. What do you make of it?
blocks.wrong: Reassure: a slow pulse is a good sign.
blocks.right: Remember the beta-blocker can hide a fast pulse: treat the low pressure as shock and call the senior.
blocks.consequence: The medicines include a beta-blocker: the heart rate cannot rise, so a slow rate with low pressure is not reassuring.
blocks.source: NICE NG253 suspected sepsis (Nov 2025, replaces NG51); Royal College of Physicians NEWS2 (2017)

blocks.title: A diabetes tablet and ketones
blocks.prompt: If the glucose looks acceptable, does that rule out a diabetic emergency?
blocks.wrong: Yes: the glucose is acceptable, so there is no diabetic emergency.
blocks.right: Check ketones and the acid balance: an SGLT2 inhibitor can cause ketoacidosis with a near-normal glucose.
blocks.consequence: The medicines include an SGLT2 inhibitor: ketoacidosis can occur with an almost normal glucose.
blocks.source: MHRA Drug Safety Update (2016, 2020) on SGLT2 inhibitors and diabetic ketoacidosis; Joint British Diabetes Societies guidance on diabetic ketoacidosis

blocks.title: An iron-deficiency pattern that is not explained
blocks.prompt: The haemoglobin is low and the red cells are small. What now?
blocks.wrong: Proceed: mild anaemia is common and needs no further work-up.
blocks.right: Find the cause (iron stores, blood loss, and the bowel in an older man or a woman past the menopause) and tell the senior; do not accept it.
blocks.consequence: The results show low iron stores or small red cells: an unexplained iron-deficiency pattern needs a cause found, not acceptance.
blocks.source: BSG guidelines for the management of iron deficiency anaemia in adults (2021); NICE NG12 suspected cancer recognition and referral

blocks.title: A fasting breach
blocks.prompt: The patient ate earlier today and the list is waiting. Do you proceed?
blocks.wrong: Proceed: the meal was some hours ago and the patient feels well.
blocks.right: Tell the anaesthetist, do not tick the fasting line as met, and let them decide on delay or a rapid sequence induction.
blocks.consequence: The history records a recent meal: the fasting rule is broken and aspiration is a risk.
blocks.source: Association of Anaesthetists / Royal College of Anaesthetists perioperative fasting guidance (2022 joint consensus); ASA practice guidelines for preoperative fasting

blocks.title: An earlier refusal that applies
blocks.prompt: The patient is now confused and the family asks you to go ahead. What do you do?
blocks.wrong: Go ahead: the family agrees and the patient cannot object now.
blocks.right: Check whether the earlier refusal is valid and applies; if it does, respect it. Involve the senior now and take legal advice if unclear.
blocks.consequence: The case records an earlier refusal made with capacity: if it is valid and applies to this treatment it binds the team even though capacity is lost; the family cannot consent for an adult.
blocks.source: Mental Capacity Act 2005 ss.24-26 (advance decisions; life-sustaining treatment needs a written, signed, witnessed statement); MCA Code of Practice ch.9; GMC Decision making and consent (2020)
